title: The Neighbor and the Stranger: Loving the People God Puts in Your Path
subtitle: Who counts as my neighbor, and who gets to be a stranger I owe nothing. The Good Samaritan, the command to love the outsider, and what it means to love across the lines that are tearing a country apart, when the person God puts in your path is exactly the one your tribe has taught you to despise.

parts.title: The Person You Were Taught to Despise
parts.body:
There is a face that rises in you when a certain word is said. A political party. A nationality. A neighborhood. A kind of person whose opinions you can predict before they open their mouth, whose presence in the comment thread makes your jaw tighten, whose bumper sticker tells you everything you need to know. You do not think of yourself as a person who hates. You think of yourself as a person with discernment. But there is a face, and when it rises, something in you closes.

Most of us live now inside a sorting machine we did not build and cannot quite see. The neighborhood, the news feed, the church, the school, the friend group, all of it quietly arranging us into people like us and people not like us, and then teaching us, gently and constantly, that the people not like us are the problem. We did not decide to despise anyone. We were formed to. The contempt arrived the way an accent arrives, absorbed from the air, and now it feels like clarity.

And here is where it gets uncomfortable for the believer. You can hold orthodox doctrine and still carry a heart that has quietly written off half the people God made. You can be right about the Trinity and wrong about the man across the street. You can sing on Sunday about a love that crossed every barrier to reach you, and drive home through a city full of barriers you have no intention of crossing. The gap between the love we received and the love we extend is the most exposed nerve in the Christian life, and most of us have learned to keep it covered.

Someone asked Jesus this exact question, and he asked it to get out of the very thing you are trying to get out of. Who is my neighbor. He was a lawyer, and he asked it, Luke says, to justify himself. He wanted a definition with an edge, a boundary line, a category of people he could love and a category he could lawfully ignore. He wanted to be told that neighbor meant the people already near him, the people like him, so that the command to love his neighbor would not cost him the stranger. We all want that ruling. We have all gone looking for it.

Jesus did not give it to him. He told a story instead, and the story took the question apart.

parts.title: What Contempt Costs
parts.body:
A country can survive disagreement. What it cannot survive is contempt, the settled conviction that the other side is not merely wrong but worthless, not mistaken but evil, not a neighbor but an obstacle. And contempt is precisely what we are now manufacturing at scale. The research has a name for it. Affective polarization, the measurable rise in how much Americans dislike, distrust, and dehumanize the people across the political line, climbing steadily for decades. We do not just disagree anymore. We loathe. And the church, which should be the one place in the country where the line is crossed, is too often the place where it is drawn hardest.

The cost lands first on actual people. The relationships that quietly ended over a vote. The family table that went silent. The friendship that cooled because someone shared the wrong post. The stranger who needed help and got a category instead. Every act of contempt is an act of unseeing, a refusal to look at a particular human face and a decision to see a type, and a person reduced to a type is a person already half abandoned. We are abandoning each other in slow motion, one unseeing at a time.

The cost lands next on the witness. The watching skeptic is not waiting to hear our argument about marriage or money or the existence of God. He is watching how we treat the people we disagree with, and he has concluded, with some evidence, that we treat them exactly the way everyone else does, only with verses. When the church mirrors the contempt of the surrounding tribe, it forfeits the one thing that ever made it strange. By this everyone will know you are my disciples, Jesus said, if you have love for one another, and the world has taken him at his word. It is checking. We are failing the check.

And the cost lands deepest on the soul of the one who despises. Contempt is corrosive to the contemptuous. It hardens the face, narrows the heart, and slowly persuades a person that their own group is righteous, which is the oldest lie and the most flattering. The man who has decided that the enemy is subhuman has, without noticing, made himself the kind of person who can do anything to them. We have seen where that ends. The twentieth century is a museum of where that ends, and it always began with ordinary people who had simply stopped seeing certain other people as fully human. I am not above that road. Neither are you. That is the point of saying it.

parts.title: Who Is My Neighbor
parts.body:
Jesus answers the lawyer with the most famous story he ever told, and it is built to detonate inside the listener. A man is beaten and left for dead on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. A priest passes by on the other side. A Levite passes by on the other side. These are the religious insiders, the people the audience expected to be the heroes, and they fail. Then comes the rescuer, and Jesus chooses the one figure his audience despised most. A Samaritan. To the Jewish ear this was not a neutral choice. Samaritans were the half-breed heretics next door, the people you crossed the road to avoid, the punchline and the enemy. Jesus made the enemy the hero on purpose.

Watch what the story does to the question. The lawyer asked who qualifies as my neighbor, hoping to draw a line around his obligation. Jesus refuses the question and replaces it with a better one. He does not tell the lawyer who his neighbor is. He shows him how to be a neighbor, and then asks which of the three was a neighbor to the man in the ditch. The lawyer cannot even say the word Samaritan. He says, the one who showed him mercy. And Jesus says, go and do likewise. The question who is my neighbor was a question about the limits of love. Jesus turns it into a question about the limits of you, and the answer is that there are none.

This is not a stray parable. It is the dense center of a theme that runs the whole length of Scripture. The law of Moses, far from being the tribal code people imagine, commanded Israel to love the foreigner. You shall love the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt. The command is grounded in memory. You know the heart of the stranger, God says, because you were one. The vulnerable outsider, the immigrant, the widow, the orphan, are named again and again as the special concern of a God who, the law says, executes justice for the fatherless and the widow and loves the stranger, giving him food and clothing. Israel was to be a nation that remembered its own rescue by sheltering the rescued.

Then the New Testament takes the whole thing and pushes it past every boundary that remained. Jesus eats with tax collectors and prostitutes, the collaborators and the unclean, the two groups a respectable man would never share a table with. He praises a Roman centurion's faith above all Israel. He lingers at a well in the heat of the day to talk theology with a Samaritan woman who has had five husbands, breaking every rule of gender, ethnicity, and respectability in a single conversation. He tells his followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them, and grounds the command in the character of the Father who sends rain on the just and the unjust. Be merciful, he says, as your Father is merciful. The standard is not the neighborhood. The standard is God.

And then comes the engine under all of it, the thing that makes the command more than moralism. While we were still enemies, Paul writes, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son. This is the gospel as the deepest possible answer to who is my neighbor. We were the stranger. We were the enemy, hostile in mind, at war with God, the very people he had every right to cross the road to avoid. And he did not pass by on the other side. He came down into the ditch, bound up our wounds at the cost of his own blood, and paid for our keeping. The Samaritan in the story is finally Christ, and the man bleeding in the road is finally us. You cannot receive that love and keep your categories. The cross is the death of the question who is my neighbor, because at the cross God treated his enemies as neighbors, and told you to go and do likewise.

parts.title: The Church That Crossed the Road
parts.body:
The strangeness of early Christian love was not a sermon. It was a smell, a sound, a fact the pagan world could not explain. In the great plagues that swept the Roman Empire in the second and third centuries, the well and the wealthy fled the cities, abandoning the sick to die alone. The Christians stayed. They nursed the dying, their own and their pagan neighbors alike, and many of them caught the disease and died doing it. The sociologist Rodney Stark argued that this ordinary mercy was a major reason the church grew, because the watching world saw a community that loved strangers at cost, and there was no category for it. The Emperor Julian, who hated the Christians and tried to revive paganism in the fourth century, complained bitterly that the godless Galileans support not only their own poor but ours as well, and that this was winning people over. He saw the threat clearly. The threat was love that crossed the road.

This was always the offense and the appeal. In the Greco-Roman world, charity flowed along lines of reciprocity and status. You helped those who could help you back. The Christian innovation, drawn straight from the parable, was care for the person who could give you nothing, the abandoned infant left exposed to die, whom Christians made a practice of rescuing and raising, the slave, the prisoner, the foreigner, the leper. The church built the first hospitals as institutions of indiscriminate mercy. Basil of Caesarea in the fourth century constructed a complex outside the city, the Basiliad, that cared for the sick and the leprous and the poor of any origin, a city of mercy that astonished the empire.

The road, of course, was crossed unevenly, and the honest history includes the failures, because the gospel keeps indicting the people who carry it. The same church that built hospitals also, in other seasons, blessed crusades, baptized empires, and turned the stranger into the infidel. The medieval persecutions of the Jews, the conquest dressed as mission, the long Christian complicity in the dehumanizing of whole peoples, are not footnotes to be skipped past. They are the church doing to the stranger exactly what the priest and the Levite did, crossing to the other side while quoting Scripture. The parable judges the church before it judges anyone else. We are in the story, and not always as the Samaritan.

Yet the deepest renewals of Christian history have almost always been recoveries of the neighbor. When the Wesleys preached in the eighteenth century, the fruit was prison reform and the slow turning of the conscience against the slave trade, a turning led by believers like William Wilberforce and the Clapham circle who could not square the trade with the parable. The abolition movement on both sides of the Atlantic was driven in large part by Christians who had finally heard the question who is my neighbor and refused the old answer. In the twentieth century, the civil rights movement in the American South was a church movement at its core, led from the pulpit, soaked in the prophets and the Sermon on the Mount, insisting that the man in the ditch and the man crossing the road were both made in the image of God. The pattern holds. When the church remembers the neighbor, it heals. When it forgets him, it harms. The history is a long commentary on a single story Jesus told on a single afternoon.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: The fracturing of trust between groups is now one of the most studied problems in the human sciences, and believers have nothing to fear from honest research into how contempt forms and how it might be undone. All truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of human division carries a hidden picture of the human person, and the picture is where the argument lives.

secular.author: Jonathan Haidt
secular.whatItGetsRight: Haidt demonstrated with care that moral judgment is largely intuitive and tribal, that we reason backward to defend conclusions our gut already reached, and that political groups bind themselves together by sacralizing certain values and demonizing those who hold others. He shows why the other side looks not merely wrong but morally blind to us, and why we are so confident in our own righteousness. The parable assumes exactly this, a lawyer reasoning backward to justify the line he already wanted to draw.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Haidt names the mechanism and cannot reach the root. Scripture agrees that the heart leads and the reason follows, but it calls the bent of that heart sin, not merely tribal wiring, and a described bias is not a healed one. Haidt can explain why you despise your opponent. He cannot get the contempt out of you, because the contempt is not finally a cognitive error to be corrected but a love disordered toward the self, and only grace reorders a love. The diagnosis is sharp. The cure is missing.

secular.author: Gordon Allport and successors
secular.whatItGetsRight: Allport's research, refined over seventy years, showed that prejudice between groups reliably decreases when people of different groups actually meet under the right conditions, working toward a shared goal as equals. Proximity dissolves the abstraction. It is much harder to despise a category once it has a face and a name and has helped you move a couch. The parable works the same way, forcing the listener to watch a despised Samaritan become a particular merciful man.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Contact is a real grace and an incomplete one. Scripture knows that proximity alone does not produce love, since the priest and the Levite were as close to the wounded man as the Samaritan was and still crossed the road. What the Samaritan had was not better information but a moved heart, compassion, the text says, the same word used of Jesus. You can put two enemies in a room and produce a more sophisticated contempt. Love requires a new heart, not only a shared task, and that is a gift the social sciences can prepare the soil for but cannot grow.

secular.source: Hospitality and the ethics of the Other
secular.author: Emmanuel Levinas
secular.whatItGetsRight: Levinas, a Jewish philosopher who survived the century that tried to erase him, built an entire ethics on the face of the Other, the claim that when you truly look at another human face you encounter an infinite demand that you not harm, that you respond, that you be responsible. The face, he said, resists possession and calls you out of yourself. This is a profound philosophical witness to the very thing contempt destroys, the particular human face that the parable forces you to see.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Levinas locates the demand in the face of the Other, and Scripture locates it one layer deeper, in the God whose image that face bears. The neighbor commands my responsibility not only because his face is infinite but because he is made in the likeness of God, and to despise him is to despise his Maker. This deepens Levinas rather than denying him, for it tells me why the face makes its claim, and it adds what he cannot, that I am able to answer the face only because Another first answered mine, descending to the ditch where I lay.

secular.source: Bowling Alone and the collapse of social capital
secular.author: Robert Putnam
secular.whatItGetsRight: Putnam documented the long decline of the associations, clubs, leagues, congregations, and civic groups that once knit Americans into a shared life across difference. As those bridges decayed, people retreated into smaller and more homogeneous circles, and the muscles of neighborliness atrophied. He shows, with sobering data, that we have built a society in which the stranger is increasingly someone we never actually meet, only imagine.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Putnam describes the emptying of the road on which the Samaritan once traveled, and his account, though true, treats community as a civic good rather than a calling. Scripture commands the neighbor whether or not the social capital is there to make it convenient. The church is meant to be the bridging institution Putnam mourns, but for a reason deeper than civic health, because it is the body of a Lord who tore down the dividing wall of hostility and made the two into one. We do not rebuild the bridges to save the republic. We rebuild them because we were strangers and were brought near.

secular.author: David Livingstone Smith
secular.whatItGetsRight: Smith's study of how humans come to see other humans as less than human, as vermin, as obstacles, as types rather than persons, traces the precise mental machinery that makes atrocity possible. He shows that dehumanization is not a failure of intelligence but a tragically normal capacity of the human mind, that ordinary people slide into it through small steps of category and contempt. This is a clear-eyed account of the road the priest and the Levite were already walking.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Smith maps the descent and cannot explain the dignity it violates, since on a purely material account there is no fixed reason the strong should not reduce the weak to vermin. Scripture supplies the floor he needs, that every human being bears the image of God and so cannot be rightly reduced to a category by anyone. And it supplies the hope he lacks, for the same gospel that names dehumanization as sin also rehumanizes the dehumanizer, giving the contemptuous a new heart that can see a face where it once saw only an obstacle.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same Scripture and the same parable still differ on how the love of neighbor should be embodied across the divisions of a polarized country, and the difference is not careless. It runs to where the energy of Christian love is best spent, in courageous engagement across the line or in the patient building of a different kind of community. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are trying to honor the Samaritan and both are guarding against a real danger.

views.view: Love by crossing the line, engaging the opponent directly
views.body: This view reads the parable as a summons to deliberate, costly contact with the very people your tribe has taught you to despise. The Samaritan did not love the wounded man from a safe distance or through an institution. He stopped, touched, paid, and returned, and Jesus said go and do likewise. So the faithful response to a fractured country is to seek out the actual neighbor across the political and cultural line, to share the table, to listen long, to refuse the algorithm that keeps you among your own. Advocates of this view argue that contempt only dies in the presence of a face, and that the church must model what the country has lost, the willingness to love someone you disagree with all the way down. They point to Jesus at the well, eating with the collaborator, praising the centurion, crossing every line in his own body. The danger they are guarding against is a Christianity that loves the neighbor in the abstract and despises him in particular, that posts about unity from inside a sealed tribe, that mistakes the warmth of agreement for the love that crosses the road. Against that they hold that love is finally a verb done to a particular face, and that a believer who never has an uncomfortable conversation across the line has not yet understood the story.

views.view: Love by building a different community, witness through a contrast people
views.body: This view reads the parable inside the larger biblical vision of the church as a new people, a community whose shared life across former divisions is itself the witness. The Samaritan acted alone on a road, but the New Testament's deeper picture is a body in which Jew and Gentile, slave and free, become one, a society that the watching world cannot explain. So the faithful response to a fractured country is to build and protect that contrast community, the local church where the lines actually dissolve, and to let its mere existence preach. Advocates of this view argue that the world is not changed first by individual heroics but by the visible reality of a people who love differently, and that a believer formed inside such a body becomes the kind of person who can cross any road. They point to the early church whose communal mercy astonished the empire and to the long history of Christian institutions of indiscriminate care. The danger they are guarding against is a Christianity exhausted by performing reconciliation for an audience while never being changed by it, that treats every relationship as a debate to win rather than a body to belong to. Against that they hold that the most subversive thing a believer can do is help build a community where the stranger is already home.

parts.title: What Loving the Stranger Forms in You
parts.body:
You do not become a neighbor by trying harder to approve of people you dislike. Approval is not the command, and willpower is not the engine. You become a neighbor slowly, as God works specific things into a heart that keeps stopping on the road, and the work is the point. The Samaritan was not displaying a personality. He was revealing a character that had been formed, and that character is what God means to form in you.

He forms sight. Contempt is a way of not seeing, of replacing a particular human being with a category and then dealing with the category, and the first thing God restores in the one who loves the stranger is the ability to actually see a face. The priest and the Levite saw a problem and a risk. The Samaritan saw a man. To be made into a neighbor is to have your eyes opened, again and again, until the abstraction breaks and the person appears, until you can no longer say them without a particular face rising to rebuke the word. This sight is not natural. It is given, and it grows in those who practice looking.

He forms freedom from the tribe. The deepest captivity of the age is not to a party but to the need for the approval of our own, and the love of the stranger is the one act that breaks it, because you cannot love the enemy your tribe has assigned you and remain fully owned by the tribe. The Samaritan crossed a line his whole people had drawn, and in doing so he showed a man whose obedience ran to a higher authority than the crowd. To be formed in this love is to be slowly set free from the tyranny of belonging, until you can be kind to the person your group hates and bear the cost of it, which is a freedom almost no one in the country currently possesses.

And he forms the likeness of Christ, which is the whole point of the Christian life. Be merciful as your Father is merciful, Jesus said, and the love of the stranger is mercy taking the exact shape of God's own mercy toward us. Every time you stop on the road for someone who can give you nothing back, someone you were taught to despise, someone who is in every way the enemy, you are doing in miniature the thing God did for you at infinite cost. You were the stranger he loved. You were the enemy he reconciled. And as you learn to love the stranger in turn, you are not merely obeying a rule. You are being conformed to the face of the One who came down into your ditch, and you carry his likeness out into a country that has forgotten there ever was such a face.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: Loving the neighbor is not a feeling you summon. It is a set of practices you take up, in small repeated acts, until the crossing of the road becomes a reflex rather than a heroic exception. None of what follows will purge your contempt by Friday. All of it will start to wear a groove if you keep at it. Begin where you are, with one thing, this week, and let the rest come as the road lengthens.

steps: Name the face that rises in you. Sit honestly with the kind of person you have quietly written off, the party, the group, the neighbor, and confess it by name to God as contempt, not discernment. You cannot repent of a sin you keep calling clarity.

Pray for one specific person on the other side of your deepest line, by name, every day. Not that they would change and agree with you. That God would bless them. Watch what praying blessing over an opponent does to your own heart.

Do one small, concrete kindness for someone who can give you nothing back and is not like you. Help the stranger move the couch, carry the bag, hold the door long enough to learn a name. Love begins in the body before it reaches the heart.

Cross one road you usually avoid in conversation. Ask a real question of someone you disagree with and listen until you could state their view in a way they would recognize, before you say a word of your own.

Read Luke 10 slowly and put yourself in every role in turn, the lawyer drawing his line, the priest crossing over, the wounded man in the ditch, and finally the Samaritan. Ask which one you most resemble this month, and do not flinch from the answer.

Audit your inputs. Notice which voices, feeds, and channels are training you in contempt, teaching you daily that the other side is subhuman, and turn down the volume on at least one of them. You are being formed by what you consume.

Build one real relationship across a line, on purpose. Take a person who is not like you to coffee, not to convert or to debate, but to know. Let the abstraction become a particular human being who has a name and a story.

Repent of the specific contempt your tribe rewards. Every group has a sin it celebrates, a hatred it calls virtue. Find yours, name it, and ask God to free you from needing your own people's approval for despising someone he made.

Practice indiscriminate mercy through your local church, joining the work it does for people who can offer nothing in return, the prisoner, the immigrant, the addict, the stranger. Let your service run along no line but need, the way the early church's did.

Find the person in your own life who is hardest to love, the family member, the neighbor, the colleague whose presence closes you, and make a season-long commitment to seek their good. The neighbor is not theoretical. He usually lives nearby.

Examine your church's witness across the divisions of the country. Is it a contrast community where the lines dissolve, or a tribe with a steeple. Have one honest conversation with your leaders about whether the dividing wall has actually come down among you.

Memorize the heart of the matter until it arrives on its own. While we were still enemies we were reconciled to God. Let the gospel of how you were loved become the engine of how you love, so the command stops feeling like a burden and starts feeling like an overflow.

Build a life whose ordinary circle is wider than your tribe. Choose, over years, to live, worship, and befriend across the lines that the country is hardening, until loving the stranger is not an event you schedule but the shape of the life you actually live.

Become a bridge for others. Use whatever standing you have, in your church, your neighborhood, your family, to bring people across the line to one another, to host the table where enemies become acquaintances and acquaintances become neighbors.

Practice the long obedience of refusing contempt even when your side is winning and the temptation to gloat is strongest. The test of neighbor love is not how you treat the opponent when you are afraid, but how you treat them when you have power.

Keep returning to the One who crossed the road for you. Read the parable for the rest of your life not as a moral to master but as a window onto the God who found you in the ditch, until the love you received and the love you extend have become, in you, the same love.
